title: Unsupervised Brain Anomaly Detection as a Bayesian Inverse Problem with Diffusion Prior

paper.title: Unsupervised Brain Anomaly Detection as a Bayesian Inverse Problem with Diffusion Prior
paper.abstract:
Abstract Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) aims to localize abnormal regions in medical scans without pixel-level annotations. A typical strategy seeks to reconstruct a pseudo-healthy image that preserves subject-specific anatomy. Recently, diffusion models have been proposed to perform UAD. However, these methods rely on heuristic noise schedules or synthetic corruptions to balance subject-specificity and anomaly removal.
In this work, we propose an alternative formulation of UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem under a diffusion prior. First, we introduce a latent spatial anomaly mask that models pixel-wise consistency between a test image and its latent corresponding pseudo-healthy image. Then, we propose an approximation of the unknown generation process that links healthy anatomy, anomalies, and the observed image, enabling a well-defined likelihood within the Bayesian framework. Building on recent advances in diffusion-based inverse problem methods, we jointly infer the pseudo-healthy image and the anomaly mask via annealed posterior sampling. We evaluate our approach on FDG PET (ADNI) and FLAIR MRI (BraTS 2021), demonstrating improved anomaly localization performance compared to other diffusion-based approaches and validating the contribution of our introduced model. Our code is available at https://github.com/HuguesRoy/UAD_DAPS .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) in medical imaging aims to identify abnormal regions without requiring assumptions about anomaly characteristics or pixel-level annotations. A common strategy is to reconstruct a pseudo-healthy version of an abnormal image to detect anomalies. Such reconstruction must satisfy two competing objectives: (i) it should be plausible under the healthy data distribution, and (ii) it should preserve subject-specific anatomical details. Diffusion models trained on healthy data have recently been used for UAD due to their strong generative capabilities. However, to balance these competing objectives, these methods rely on heuristic choices, such as denoising noise levels [ 1 , 3 , 4 , 23 ] , corruption strategies [ 4 , 22 , 24 , 18 ] , or synthetic anomalies [ 11 , 13 , 2 ] . In parallel, diffusion models recently achieved strong performance in Bayesian inverse problems by leveraging learned data priors [ 19 , 25 ] . These approaches progressively estimate a latent clean signal from noisy observations through iterative denoising updates. However, they rely on a known forward model linking the clean signal to the noisy measurement, which is unavailable in UAD. In this work, we bridge these two lines of research by formulating unsupervised anomaly detection as a Bayesian inverse problem in which the forward model is unknown and must be approximated. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) we formulate diffusion-based UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem with a latent anomaly mask; (2) we introduce an approximation of the unknown forward model; (3) we propose a spatially regularized mask prior enabling stable joint inference via intermediate posterior sampling [ 25 ] ; and (4) we conduct extensive experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach which outperforms existing diffusion-based methods on both PET and MRI benchmarks.

sections.heading: 2 Inverse problem using diffusion models
sections.text: Inverse problems aim to reconstruct an unknown signal 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} from a partial, noisy measurement 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} by inverting a known forward model that describes the measurement process. In a Bayesian setting, reconstruction is formulated as inference under the posterior distribution p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒚 ) ∝ p ⁡ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 ) ​ p ​ ( 𝒙 0 ) p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{y})\propto p(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0})p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}) , where the likelihood p ⁡ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 ) p(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0}) is defined by the forward model and p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}) is the prior distribution. A key challenge of inverse problems is to approximate this unknown prior. Recently, diffusion models have shown strong performance to approximate priors [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 12 , 19 ] in inverse problems. A noisy signal 𝒙 t \boldsymbol{x}_{t} is iteratively denoised using both a prior diffusion model trained on clean signals and the likelihood p ⁡ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 t ) p(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{t}) , leading to a denoising process conditioned on the measurement 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} . However, early denoising errors have been found to be difficult to correct [ 25 ] . To address this limitation, Zhang et al. [ 25 ] proposed the Decoupled Annealed Posterior Sampling (DAPS) strategy. Rather than strictly following the diffusion trajectory, DAPS introduces a sequence of intermediate posteriors p k ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒚 , 𝒙 t k ) ∝ p ⁡ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 ) ​ p k ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t k ) p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}})\propto p(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0})p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}}) which gradually converge to the true posterior p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒚 ) p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{y}) and enable exploring a larger solution space. As in [ 6 , 19 ] , they approximate the conditional prior p k ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t k ) p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}}) using a Gaussian distribution, p k ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t k ) ≈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 ^ 0 ​ ( 𝒙 t k , t k ) , r k 2 ​ 𝑰 ) , p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}})\approx\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{x}_{0};\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}},t_{k}),r_{k}^{2}\boldsymbol{I}\right), (1) where 𝒙 ^ 0 \hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0} is sampled from the reverse process of the diffusion model. The variance r k 2 r_{k}^{2} weights the contribution of the conditional prior in the intermediate posterior. Instead of directly sampling 𝒙 t k + 1 \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k+1}} from 𝒙 t k \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}} , an intermediate signal 𝒙 0 ( k ) \boldsymbol{x}_{0}^{(k)} is sampled using the intermediate posterior p k ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒚 , 𝒙 t k ) p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}}) and re-noised to obtain a sample 𝒙 t k + 1 \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k+1}} . Thanks to this decoupled sampling strategy and intermediate posterior parameterization, larger changes between iterations are obtained, preventing early denoising errors from propagating through the sampling process. A key limitation of DAPS and other inverse problem approaches is their reliance on a known and available forward model. This assumption typically does not hold in unsupervised anomaly detection for medical imaging, where no forward model exists to sample an abnormal image 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} from a healthy image 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} .

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: In this work, we propose a new diffusion-based approach to unsupervised anomaly detection. Specifically, we formulate anomaly detection as a Bayesian inverse problem and approximate the unknown forward model by introducing a latent variable 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} that represents a probabilistic anomaly mask. Under this formulation, the objective is to jointly infer the healthy image 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} and the mask 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} from the observed image 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} . In the following sections, we define the probabilistic model, including the likelihood, the priors, and the proposed inference strategy. Figure 1: Top left: Probabilistic graphical model of the proposed method. Right: Overview of the inference process. As k k increases, the posterior distribution progressively concentrates, enabling the sampling of the final estimates 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} and 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} . The variable 𝒙 t k \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}} denotes the noisy version of 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} at step k k , which allows a decoupling between the previously sampled noisy variable and the newly generated one.

sections.heading: Generative model
sections.text: To formalize anomaly detection as a Bayesian inverse problem, we assume that the observed image 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} is generated from a latent healthy image 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} and a latent anomaly mask 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} through the likelihood p ⁡ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 ) p(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m}) . Specifically, the observation 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} is expected to coincide with 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} only in regions labeled as normal by the mask 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} . As shown in the graphical model in Fig. 1 , assuming prior independence between 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} and 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} , the joint distribution factorizes as p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 , 𝒚 ) = p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) ​ p ​ ( 𝒎 ) ​ p ​ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 ) , p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{y})=p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0})p(\boldsymbol{m})p(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m}), where p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}) is the prior over healthy images and p ⁡ ( 𝒎 ) p(\boldsymbol{m}) is a spatial prior over anomaly masks. As in Bayesian inverse problems, the objective is to sample the healthy image 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} and anomaly mask 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} from the posterior p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 ∣ 𝒚 ) ∝ p ⁡ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 ) ​ p ​ ( 𝒙 0 ) ​ p ​ ( 𝒎 ) p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m}\mid\boldsymbol{y})\propto p(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m})p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0})p(\boldsymbol{m}) . To approximate this posterior, we adopt a similar formulation as in DAPS [ 25 ] . Introducing the noisy diffusion states 𝒙 t k \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}} to approximate the image prior p ⁡ ( 𝒙 0 ) p(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}) , we define a sequence of intermediate posteriors p k ( 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 ∣ 𝒚 , 𝒙 t k ) ∝ p k ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 ) p k ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t k ) p ( 𝒎 ) , \displaystyle p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m}\mid\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}})\propto p_{k}(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m})\,p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}})\,p(\boldsymbol{m}), (2) where p k ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t k ) p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}}) is the conditional diffusion prior defined in Eq. sections.heading: Approximate the forward model
sections.text: Unlike classical inverse problems, the forward model relating a healthy image 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} to an abnormal scan 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} is unknown. In this section, we propose an approximation of the forward model p ⁡ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 ) p(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m}) based on the introduced anomaly mask 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} . The probabilistic anomaly mask 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} encodes pixel-level abnormality: values close to 0 indicate anomalous measurements, whereas values close to 1 enforce consistency between 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} and 𝒙 0 \boldsymbol{x}_{0} . Accordingly, we model the likelihood as: p k ​ ( 𝒚 ∣ 𝒙 0 , 𝒎 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒚 , 𝒙 0 , r k 2 ​ diag ​ ( 𝒎 ) − 2 ) , \displaystyle p_{k}(\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{m})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{y};\boldsymbol{x}_{0},r_{k}^{2}\,\mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{m})^{-2})\kern 5.0pt, (3) with variance r k 2 r_{k}^{2} , matched to the conditional prior p k ​ ( 𝒙 0 ∣ 𝒙 t k ) p_{k}(\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}}) variance. This ensures that, at intermediate step k k , in normal regions, the variability of the diffusion-based prediction is consistent with the variability observed in 𝒚 \boldsymbol{y} . Deviations exceeding this expected variability cannot be explained by the prior and are therefore attributed to abnormal regions.

sections.heading: Spatial prior on the mask
sections.text: Since the probabilistic mask 𝒎 \boldsymbol{m} is introduced as a latent variable, we must specify a prior distribution p ⁡ ( 𝒎 ) p(\boldsymbol{m}) . To enforce values in ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) , we parametrize it as 𝒎 = s ⁡ ( 𝒂 ) \boldsymbol{m}=s(\boldsymbol{a}) , where 𝒂 \boldsymbol{a} are unconstrained logits and s s denotes the sigmoid function. We then define a prior p ⁡ ( 𝒂 ) p(\boldsymbol{a}) , that (i) defines the initial mask value, (ii) controls the magnitude of mask updates during inference, and (iii) enforces spatial consistency. To this end, we assume a Gaussian Markov random field prior: p ⁡ ( 𝒂 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝒂 , μ ​ 𝟏 , 𝑸 − 1 ) , \displaystyle p(\boldsymbol{a})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{a};\mu\boldsymbol{1},\boldsymbol{Q}^{-1})\kern 5.0pt, (4) with a precision matrix 𝑸 = λ 0 ​ 𝑰 + λ c ​ 𝑳 \boldsymbol{Q}=\lambda_{0}\boldsymbol{I}+\lambda_{c}\boldsymbol{L} , where λ 0 , λ c > 0 \lambda_{0},\lambda_{c}>0 and 𝑳 \boldsymbol{L} is the graph Laplacian of the image grid. The quadratic form 𝒂 ⊤ ​ 𝑳 ​ 𝒂 \boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{L}\boldsymbol{a} penalizes differences between neighboring logits, promoting spatial consistency. The parameter μ \mu sets the initial value of the mask, λ 0 \lambda_{0} controls the global shrinkage of logits toward μ \mu , and λ c \lambda_{c} governs the spatial consistency strength.

If the prior weight λ 0 \lambda_{0} is kept fixed across intermediate steps, this changing scale alters the balance between the likelihood and the logit prior. sections.heading: Implementation details
sections.text: We adopt the diffusion parameterization of Karras et al. [ 10 ] and train the diffusion model exclusively on healthy data. The conditional estimate 𝒙 ^ 0 ​ ( 𝒙 t k , t k ) \hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{k}},t_{k}) in Eq. ( 1 ) is obtained using the probability flow ordinary differential equation [ 20 ] (PF-ODE) with two solver steps per noise level. For all experiments, we use 150 intermediate posterior steps in the DAPS framework and 75 Langevin iterations at each intermediate step. The noise levels { t k } \{t_{k}\} follow the DAPS parameterization with σ max = 20 \sigma_{\max}=20 . We set the spatial consistency parameters λ c \lambda_{c} to 1. An 80GB NVIDIA H100 GPU was used for training.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments & Results
sections.text: To evaluate the performance of our proposed model, experiments were conducted on 2D FLAIR MRI of glioblastoma patients and on 2D FDG PET with synthetic Alzheimer-like hypometabolism. Our framework was compared with UAD diffusion models [ 3 , 4 , 24 ] and state of the art methods [ 9 , 11 , 13 ] . For the proposed approach, we use the inferred latent anomaly mask directly as anomaly maps, while other methods use residuals. Datasets ADNI PET FDG PET images were obtained from ADNI [ 16 ] and preprocessed with Clinica [ 17 ] (affine registration to MNI, intensity normalization, cropping, resampling to 128 3 128^{3} , rescaling to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] ). We selected 621 images from 301 cognitively normal subjects. Fifty images were kept for testing. Because no ground truth exists, we use the framework described in [ 8 ] to generate synthetic images with Alzheimer-like hypometabolism (50%). The remaining images were split at the subject level into training (545) and validation (25 volumes) sets. BRATS FLAIR FLAIR images from BraTS 2021 [ 15 ] and ADNI [ 16 ] were preprocessed with Clinica [ 17 ] in a similar manner as the PET images. Models were trained on healthy ADNI FLAIR slices (234 subjects) and evaluated on BraTS slices containing tumors (1,251 subjects). To analyze sensitivity to anomaly size, slices were grouped into medium and large categories using the 33 rd and 66 th percentiles of lesion area. One slice per subject was randomly selected per category, yielding 819 large lesions and 1,156 medium lesions. Evaluation For the PET images, because multiple slices come from the same subject, we account for this hierarchical structure using stratified bootstrapping at the subject level when computing metrics. We also report the inference time. Detection performance was evaluated using the best possible Dice score ( ⌈ Dice ⌉ \lceil\text{Dice}\rceil ) and pixel-wise average precision (AP). Significance was assessed via Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons ( p < 0.01 p<0.01 ). Baselines We compare our method to diffusion-based UAD approaches, including AnoDDPM [ 24 ] (G-Gaussian and S-simplex noise variants), AutoDDPM (Gaussian noise) [ 3 ] , and THOR (Simplex noise) [ 4 ] . For fairness, all diffusion models use the same U-Net backbone. We additionally compare against IterMask 2 \text{IterMask}^{2} [ 13 ] , a recent state-of-the-art UAD framework that uses synthetic anomalies, and a variational autoencoder ( β \beta - VAE ) [ 9 , 14 ] . sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In summary, we formulated unsupervised anomaly detection as a Bayesian inverse problem, using a diffusion model as a prior over healthy anatomy. Our method introduces a latent anomaly mask that is inferred jointly with the reconstruction through sampling of a sequence of intermediate posteriors. The mask provides an approximation of the unknown forward model, while a spatial prior ensures coherent and anatomically consistent anomaly regions. Ablation studies confirmed the importance of each proposed component. Experimentally, our model achieves competitive performance on BraTS and state-of-the-art results on ADNI PET compared to multiple baselines. While the current formulation already demonstrates competitive performance, it also opens several directions for further development. Replacing the Gaussian approximation of the conditional diffusion prior with a more expressive model could improve the approximation of the intermediate posteriors and enhance anomaly detection. Similarly, refining the forward model formulation may allow the framework to better capture pathological patterns. Since our method relies on joint intermediate posterior inference, alternative sampling or optimization strategies may improve stability and computational efficiency. Extending the framework to full 3D volumes is another important direction. Together, these improvements would extend the framework to other imaging modalities and clinical problems.
